prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the development of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists that transformed treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings placed B007 first, and I agree on the science: it is a complete arc from peptide physiology (proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic and satiety actions of GLP-1, receptor biology) to a drug class with replicated outcome-trial benefit in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. Maturity is not in doubt. The attribution problem is the three-person cap, not the merit. Holst and Drucker anchor the physiology and its translation. For the third place I still favour Knudsen, because without long-acting acylated analogues the physiology would not have become a medicine, and a prize that stops at the hormone would leave the therapeutic half of the achievement unrecognised.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a single crowded prize forces us to omit either Mojsov, whose identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is credited in four colleagues' openings, or Knudsen, whose industrial development is the step that delivered the therapy. Either omission can be criticised as unfair, and I have not verified the priority dispute around Mojsov myself, only the credit supplied. A second concern is that a physiology-to-industry configuration may look to some like honouring a commercial product rather than a discovery, and long-term safety and durability of obesity treatment are still accruing.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks B007 first with Mojsov rather than Knudsen, arguing that discovery-level contributions should be favoured within the three-person limit and that Knudsen's role is chiefly pharmaceutical development; he also places B004 second as a clean, mechanistic two-person discovery.
responses.response: I take the discovery-first principle seriously and it is the most reasonable counter to my choice. But the Medicine prize has repeatedly recognised the step that makes a discovery usable by patients, and here that step is distinctive and original, not routine engineering: fatty-acid acylation to bind albumin and give once-daily and once-weekly dosing. My difficulty with Mojsov is that her contribution rests on a credit I cannot verify from the supplied text and is entangled with other early contributors, while Knudsen's is documented in approved drugs. I will keep the question open and would move if the committee judges the peptide identification to be more decisive than I currently do. On B004, I agree it is clean and fundamental, and I rate it highly as a fallback, though its clinical consequence is still emerging.

responses.point: Linnarsson favours the basic-discovery trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for B007 and ranks CAR-T second with only June and Sadelain, leaving Rosenberg outside because adoptive cell therapy overlaps with other territory.
responses.response: I agree that the basic-versus-industrial choice is the real fault line in B007. Where I differ is that excluding Knudsen makes the citation read as a physiology prize only, while the justification for honouring this field is the medicines. On B041 I find his two-person version more defensible than the three-name version in several openings, because it avoids implying that Rosenberg's adoptive transfer work is the same achievement as CAR design. But Eshhar's absence from the supplied credit remains a serious problem for any CAR-T configuration, and that is why I keep B041 as an alternative and not my preferred prize.

responses.point: Sandberg proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for B007 and ranks B002 third with Hall and Schreiber, excluding Sabatini because of the ambiguity of his record.
responses.response: I share his B007 configuration and his reasoning for the cap. On B002 I am more cautious: Hall's discovery of TOR is clearly central, but pairing him with Schreiber rests on the FKBP12-rapamycin chemistry rather than on growth control itself, and pairing him with Sabatini raises a reputational question that I cannot assess from the evidence supplied. Because there is no clean second name, I rank B002 lower than he does and do not propose it as an alternative.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius also places B007 first with Mojsov and sees B041 second, but values anti-TNF therapy and the Cory, Adams and Vaux BCL-2 work, which are not among the ballots I may discuss.
responses.response: I note her emphasis on candidates with a very clear mechanism-to-proof logic, and I accept that criterion for judging B007 and B041, where the mechanism-to-clinic chain is also strong. Within the shortlist, it argues for B004 as the cleanest mechanistic alternative. I disagree only if the criterion is used to prefer a prize with a narrower clinical footprint over B007, whose clinical evidence base is substantially larger.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will weight physiology and peptide identification (Mojsov) or pharmaceutical development (Knudsen) as the third name for B007.
The priority history around the active GLP-1 peptide, which I have not verified beyond the credited names.
Whether Eshhar and other early CAR contributors outside the credited list make B041 unusable in a three-name form.
Whether a two-part configuration would be preferable to a single crowded prize given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I worked with Paul Greengard as a postdoctoral fellow and have co-authored with committee colleague Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neuron topics, but neither relationship involves a shortlisted candidate or the achievements discussed.
